source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC), appendix Tables 4-5
finding: Re-read full paper. The headline 20% is pass@2 on the 400-task public evaluation set at 2000 steps. It is a per-puzzle code-length minimiser (VAE-style, bits-back) run on the puzzle only.
numbers: 76K parameters. Eval set pass@1/2/5/10/100 at 2000 steps: 18.5/20.0/24.25/26.0/31.25%; pass@2 peaks at 21.5% at 1500 steps. Training set pass@2 34.75% at 2000 steps. Total time 138 h for 400 eval puzzles on one RTX 4070 (about 20.7 min per puzzle); 130 h for 400 training puzzles. Eval pass@2 at 100/200/500/1000 steps: 1.25/6.0/15.0/19.25%. U-Net baseline trained on the target puzzle only: 0.75%.
limits: Compression is the generator here, not a ranker of external candidates. Pass@1000 reaches 33.75% but no rule for choosing guesses was found in the text.
agent_relevance: Verified. Per-puzzle cost is about 20 GPU-minutes, so code-length minimisation is a heavy solver, not a cheap S7 tie-break. The score keeps rising until about 1500 steps.

finding: Re-read evaluation. Verified 69 fit and 57 correct. Search efficiency and the head-to-head with Icecuber added.
numbers: 400 public eval tasks: 69 fit all training pairs, 57 correct on all tests (82% generalisation), 53 of 57 correct on first attempt. Stricter all-test count: MADIL 59 correct vs Icecuber 117; overlap 43; 16 solved only by MADIL. MCTS with 180 s budget per task; 177 models visited on average over the 400 tasks, 28.7 final models; best model has average rank 1.6 among final models (1.3 on the 69 solved tasks). Author states 80% of solutions come within 20 s.
quote: the risk to find spurious expressions rises when there are fewer training examples, and when allowing for larger expressions
limits: Candidates are MADIL's own, not LLM-proposed. The rank of the best model among final models is measured by description length plus search, so it is partly circular.
agent_relevance: Verified. Inside its own search the shortest fit is usually the best found model, yet spurious fits remain its main generalisation failure (d03).

finding: MADIL's author says the main cause of fits that fail on the test input is spurious expressions that compensate for wrong decompositions. He calls for revising expression lengths and the balance between model and data cost.
numbers: 21 training tasks have a fit that is wrong on some or all test inputs. Of 62 unsolved-but-solvable training tasks, 21 need non-compressive steps (shorter route does not lead to the solution) and 15 fail because top-K descriptions are not diverse.
limits: Qualitative inspection by one author on training tasks. No sweep of the data-versus-model weight reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Direct ARC evidence for gap 3: with few examples a length term may be mis-weighted; argues for a tunable weight and held-out checks. Strict compression can also block the path to the right answer.

source: Li et al. (2024) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Measures how often programs that fit all training pairs are wrong on the test input, which bounds how much a tie-break among fitting programs can help. Majority vote over test outputs is their selection rule.
numbers: About 9% of sampled programs that fit the training examples are false positives. Of the problems with false positives, about half have most fitting samples still giving the correct output, so majority vote removes them. Validation 2-try accuracy (ARC-Heavy BARC models): induction with 10k samples and majority vote 19.25%; transduction without TTT 37.50%; ensemble without TTT 29.75%. Selection in section 4: filter by train fit, then pick uniformly at random among fitting programs.
limits: No shortest-program rule was tested. Fine-tuned BARC models, not general LLMs. Rates are per sample and per problem as described, not per token budget.
agent_relevance: Sets an upper bound for gap 1. Majority vote among fitting programs already removes about half of the false-positive problems, leaving a small slice where a length tie-break could add anything. The equal-token comparison itself is untested.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search (ICLR), re-read for selection
finding: Programs correct on all examples almost always generalise, so execution verification is the main selector; no length rule is used. Having a correct hypothesis in the set is the bottleneck.
numbers: ARC subset: direct 17%, program-only 23%, summarised hypotheses 30%, human-selected 33%. 64 hypotheses, 8 programs each, 3 rounds of execution feedback. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for only 49 tasks. Of 30 tasks solved with summarised hypotheses, 28 already had a correct hypothesis before summarising.
limits: Authors report a low false-positive rate. No length, random-order or vote ablation.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 1 partly: verify-then-first-fit is already strong. Any length tie-break acts only after that gate and only on rare ties.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal Yet Puzzling (ICLR)
finding: Hypothesis generate-select-refine with a symbolic interpreter beats plain sampling with majority vote. Selection uses accuracy on the exemplars, and the authors flag overfitting to exemplars.
numbers: Text: sampling more and taking a majority vote (self-consistency) 'does not necessarily improve performance', while more hypotheses with selection do. Replacing the interpreter with the LM degrades performance substantially. On MiniSCAN, T=3 N=1 beat T=3 N=5, which they link to exemplar overfitting.
limits: Numbers are in figures only. GPT-4-class models on small rule tasks. No description-length selection.
agent_relevance: Verification-based selection beats vote for rule induction. The MiniSCAN note is a small hint that fit-only selection can choose the wrong hypothesis, the case a length penalty targets.

source: Hewitt and Liang (2019) Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks
finding: Read directly. Selectivity is linguistic-task accuracy minus control-task accuracy, where the control task gives random labels per word type. A probe that can memorise random labels is not reading the representation. Simple probes are more selective.
numbers: ELMo layer 1 part-of-speech: linear 97.2 task / 71.2 control / 26.0 selectivity; MLP-1 97.3 / 92.8 / 4.5; MLP-2 97.3 / 93.2 / 4.2. Tuning MLP-1 for selectivity raised it from 4.5 to 16.6. Layer 2 linear probe: 96.6 accuracy, selectivity 31.4 vs 26.0 for layer 1.
limits: Accuracy-based, no code lengths. Voita and Titov (2020) treat MDL as the cleaner version of this idea.
agent_relevance: Closes the Hewitt and Liang part of gap 9. A control-task style check (does the explanation also fit scrambled labels) is a cheap sanity test for a candidate hypothesis.

source: Gruenwald and Roos (2019) Minimum Description Length Revisited, sections 1 and 6.3
finding: Secondary account of Rissanen 1978: it coined MDL and used two-part codes on discretised countable sets, with the complexity term approximated as zero. Also states the misspecification result and the repair by a learning rate eta below 1.
numbers: Gruenwald and Langford 2007: constructed cases where MDL picks a suboptimal model for all large n. Gruenwald and van Ommen 2017: same in linear regression, and with finitely many models a bad model can be chosen even at relatively large n. De Heide 2016: also on real data sets. Repair: raise the likelihood to the power eta, usually eta < 1.
quote: MDL (and Bayesian inference) can become inconsistent
limits: Rissanen 1978 itself (Automatica, paywalled) was not opened.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 9. For gap 3: a damped weight is a published repair, but only for probabilistic model classes, not for LLM-proposed hypothesis sets.

source: Gruenwald and van Ommen (2014/2017) Inconsistency of Bayesian Inference for Misspecified Linear Models
finding: Original arXiv version read for the setup. Homoskedastic linear models fit to heteroskedastic data: the posterior moves onto ever higher-dimensional models as n grows, with bad squared-error risk. SafeBayes learns eta from the data and picks small eta once the posterior is not concentrated.
numbers: Nested polynomial models; the best-in-class model lies in M0 and has substantial prior mass, yet posterior mass moves to larger p as n increases. With ridge regression Bayes recovers only at a sample size 'incomparably larger' than under a correct model. Exact risk values are in figures and were not extracted.
limits: Synthetic regression with a fixed model family. Does not cover discrete hypothesis choice by LLMs.
agent_relevance: Supports claim K02 as established for regression. The link to the agent is by analogy only: when the true rule is outside the proposal set, a plain length tie-break may favour wrong complex explanations.

source: Wu et al. (2023) Self-Adaptive ICL, scale and limitation sections
finding: Re-read for replication information. No independent replication was found. The paper reports OPT 350M to 175B and other 1.3-1.7B models on a few tasks, with gains over baselines, and states two limits.
numbers: Main table is GPT2-XL (1.5B) only. OPT scaling was shown for SST-2, SNLI and Commonsense QA in figures: SST-2 plateaus after 1.3B; on SNLI a 30B OPT beats the 175B. Limits: gains shrink when the retrieval set is smaller; TopK helps only on simple NLU with small label spaces, not on QA, multi-choice or NLG.
limits: Figure values not extracted. No 2024-2026 model replication found, but search tools were blocked (d17), so absence is weak.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. The MDL score is a label-confidence signal that needs a closed label set, a poor fit for open-ended agent hypotheses.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Compression Represents Intelligence Linearly, method section
finding: Re-read how bits per character is made comparable: token loss summed and divided by characters, and context windows unified to 1900 tokens with a sliding window. Models differ in tokenizer, size and family.
numbers: 31 public LLMs, 12 benchmarks, Pearson about -0.95 per domain and -0.93 overall; HellaSwag -0.881, TriviaQA -0.951, MMLU -0.890. Aligned (fine-tuned) models are excluded because they are no longer general-purpose compressors. Outliers are flagged as likely benchmark overfitting.
limits: Base models only, in-domain corpora, English-centred. Yuan et al. 2025 (linguistic bias) was not located or read.
agent_relevance: Part answer to gap 5: bits per character is tokenizer-normalised by design and held across families. It ranks base models, but is not shown usable per run inside an agent.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression, section 3.6
finding: Tokenizer choice changes the raw compression rate, and the direction depends on model size: small models gain from larger BPE vocabularies, bigger models do not.
numbers: Transformers trained on enwik8, raw rate on enwik9 for 200K / 6.4M / 38M parameter models. ASCII (no tokenization): 22.9 / 13.6 / 6.4 percent. BPE rows are partly garbled in the text extraction; the last row (likely BPE 20K) reads 19.3 / 16.4 / 9.0, so at 38M parameters ASCII (6.4) beats BPE. The text says small models improve with more tokens and bigger models worsen.
limits: Use the direction, not individual cells. Trained on enwik8 only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: compression numbers are not tokenizer-stable. A cheap bits-per-character proxy inside the agent must fix one model and tokenizer and compare only within it.

source: Kolmogorov-Test authors (2025) The Kolmogorov Test, Table 1
finding: Re-read Table 1: zero-shot code generation of the shortest program for a sequence. Accuracy is low on real modalities and generated programs are longer than gzip.
numbers: Accuracy for length-128 sequences. Llama-3.1-8B: Audio-16 5.9, Audio-8 3.9, MFCC 8.8, DNA 3.7, Text 1.4, Synthetic 8.5. Llama-3.1-405B: 18.0 / 10.1 / 24.2 / 22.5 / 9.6 / 18.0. GPT-4o: 35.6 / 15.0 / 29.6 / 24.8 / 6.5 / 33.3, precision 1.58 to 3.17 (longer than gzip). Trained SeqCoder-1.5B: 69.5 / 36.4 / 83.8 / 50.3 / 54.2 / 44.7. Chain of thought changed Llama accuracy by -1.3 (8B), -5.1 (70B), +2.1 (405B) on average.
limits: Exact output of the sequence is required. Numeric sequences, not ARC.
agent_relevance: Asking an LLM to write the shortest description directly is unreliable. Measure length on candidates it proposed instead.

source: Gao et al. (2026) RIMRULE, Tables 2, 4 and 8
finding: Re-read. MDL consolidation is compared only with prompt-based LLM merging, not with pruning by recency or usage. Gains on the unseen split are within one standard deviation.
numbers: ToolHop: test-rand 27.6 (rule generation only) to 31.1 (consolidated, 72 rules); test-unseen 42.1 to 43.1. BFCL: test-rand 54.8 to 56.6, test-unseen 47.6 to 48.5, rules 151 to 121. Standard deviations 1.2 to 1.6. Table 8 (test-rand): prompt-based consolidation 27.5 vs MDL-guided 31.1 on ToolHop, 52.1 vs 56.6 on BFCL. Low-data case with 90 samples: unseen 46.0 to 60.0.
limits: Table text extraction is garbled on rule counts; check against the PDF before quoting counts. No recency, usage or frequency baseline. Unseen gains of +1.0 and +0.9 are smaller than the SD.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. The MDL step beats LLM-based merging in distribution, but its edge on unseen tasks is not shown to be real. Claim K19 needs this caveat.

source: Elmoznino et al. (2025) In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor, appendix C.4
finding: Read the GPT-4 protocol. gpt-4o was run at temperature 0 with logprobs, one new example at a time with a growing context, which already emulates prequential coding. So sequential prediction was used, and it did not rescue the model.
numbers: Task: secret 8-digit code, digits 0-5, answer is two numbers (right place, right digit). Structured prompt with one worked demo; up to 10 retries on format failure. Result: GPT-4 cross-entropy far above small meta-trained ICL models and above the marginal-label baseline, 5 seeds.
limits: No ablation on prompt format, chain of thought or fine-tuning. The two-number feedback task may be beyond in-context ability, which would not be an Occam failure. Cross-entropy comes from output-token logprobs.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 only partly answered: sequential prompting is not the fix, and scale is not the cause (gpt-4o is large). Lack of meta-training or plain task difficulty remain candidates, untested.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: Context for cost. Top solutions use LLM-guided program synthesis and test-time training; brute-force DSL search is a strong baseline. The report does not mention a compression ranker.
numbers: Private eval state of the art rose from 33% to 55.5%. Greenblatt reached 42% on the public eval with GPT-4o program sampling. Brute-force DSL search reached 20% on the private set. The report says a score should be read as approach plus compute budget.
limits: Public and private sets differ. Dollar figures per task were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Cost frame for gap 6: CompressARC (about 20 GPU-minutes, 20% eval) and MADIL (180 s budget, 57/400 correct) score well below LLM pipelines. Using compression to rank LLM candidate programs is not tested in anything I could open.

source: Gap search note: search tools blocked
finding: WebSearch quota was exhausted at the start; arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all returned rate-limit errors. Only papers with known arXiv ids or direct URLs could be opened. Yuan et al. 2025, any direct LLM+MDL selection benchmark, and any 2024-2026 replication of Wu et al. could not be searched for.
limits: Negative results for gaps 1, 2, 4 and 5 mean not found with these tools, not that no such work exists.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2 and 4 need a new search pass after quota resets, or a direct experiment in our own harness.
